Numerous numerical methods for resolving configurational degrees of freedom in complex systems are based on the molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo principles. Despite the utility of these techniques, they often fall short in accurately capturing slow configurational changes due to their reliance on Brownian or Eulerian time advancements. To address this limitation, we present a new method called 'Configuration Tuning via Langevin Dynamics' that directly samples desired conformations through a more efficient, drift-enhanced Langevin dynamics approach. By avoiding the need for force evaluations at desired conformation times, this method can accurately resolve large configurational jumps without the usual diffusion timescale constraints. Following the application of the new method to a variety of complex systems, including polymeric materials and proteins, we observed significant improvements in configurational sampling efficiency compared to traditional methods. In one example system, a polymeric chain with 60 repeat units was found to sample configurations with a precision three orders of magnitude greater than molecular dynamics simulations of the same system. The results highlight the potential of the 'Configuration Tuning via Langevin Dynamics' approach to tackle a wide range of complex systems that are challenging to model using existing methods. The code for the new algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub to facilitate its use within the molecular dynamics community. The code can be found at https://github.com/CompPhysAlgorithms/CTL. The paper also includes a user guide to aid in the implementation of the new method. Researchers have developed hydrodynamic theories for quantum gases that rely on second-order velocity and density gradients appearing in the equation of motion before they can describe superfluid behavior. To address this, we propose a new random phase-space hydrodynamic approach for interacting Bose gases that bypasses the need for gradient orders beyond one. By incorporating quantum noise terms into the equation of motion, our method effectively captures superfluid behavior and its associated phenomena without the need for a small momentum current assumption. We further validated the theory's validity by deriving hydrodynamic equations for a single-component Bose-Einstein condensate in a $d$-dimensional system under the Bogoliubov regime and identified the conditions necessary for the theory's applicability. Finally, we applied the new framework to investigate non-equilibrium superfluid flow scenarios in one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems. The resulting dynamics showed excellent agreement with quantum field theory predictions and demonstrated the approach's capability in describing both homogeneous and inhomogeneous current patterns within the condensate. The phase-space random hydrodynamic method offers a powerful toolset for studying quantum hydrodynamics in superfluid gases by allowing researchers to avoid non-trivial current assumptions and extending existing theories to more complex situations. The developed approach also provides a foundation for further research into other low-temperature quantum systems and their behavior within hydrodynamic descriptions. The methodology presented in this paper is highly versatile and can be applied to various systems by simply substituting existing equations of motion for the conserved density field. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that even seemingly random natural processes can mask underlying patterns of behavior that become visible with the right analysis.
